prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, bringing frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: B012 is the cleanest fit to the criterion of a discovery or invention of great benefit: a single, clearly stated idea (cancelling the lattice light shift at a magic wavelength so that many neutral atoms can be interrogated on a narrow transition without Doppler or recoil shifts) that has been turned into an instrument at roughly 1e-18 fractional uncertainty. It has been reproduced and compared by independent laboratories on several continents, so the result does not depend on one group, and it is already being used for relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and the preparation of a redefinition of the second. Attribution is workable with two names, Katori for the concept and early strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking accuracy, coherence and applications to the record level. I rated it first in my opening ballot and, after reading the colleagues' ballots, I still hold it first: four of us placed it first and six placed it in the top three, and the support comes from the atomic physicists and from Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce who do not work on clocks.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the 2005 prize (frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (control of single trapped ions) already sit next to this field, so the committee could argue that precision frequency metrology has been honoured and that clocks are an application of those advances. A second is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the full impact is still prospective. A third is credit: other lattice-clock groups (for example the Tokyo/RIKEN, PTB, SYRTE and NIST efforts and the ytterbium clocks) made decisive contributions that two names cannot capture. I also declare a bias: as an atomic physicist I may overrate a result that is close to my own subject, and the opening ballots show that B042 has a case with comparable breadth in condensed matter.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked DMFT (B008) first and placed the optical lattice clocks only eighth, noting that the field is outside his core expertise, that the redefinition of the second is still pending, and that the 2005 comb prize and Wineland's 2012 prize may complicate novelty.
responses.response: I accept that the redefinition has not happened, but I do not think a prize should wait for a regulatory step. The scientific achievement, 1e-18 uncertainty reproduced in several laboratories, is established regardless of what the General Conference on Weights and Measures decides. On novelty I disagree: the comb prize recognised the measurement of optical frequencies and the 2012 prize the control of single quantum systems, whereas the magic-wavelength lattice is a different idea, state-independent trapping of many atoms, which is what moved stability and accuracy together. I would also push back on B008 as a first choice for this year: Eriksson himself notes that its accuracy for nonlocal correlations is limited, and a method-based theory prize rests on demonstrated predictive impact that I find easier to cite for a measured quantity than for a numerical framework. I do take seriously that I cannot judge DMFT from my own field and that Eriksson is the right person to weigh it.

responses.point: Pearce ranked magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B042) first, with the clocks second, arguing that the flat-band prediction plus the 2018 experiments created a large and original field with independent reproduction.
responses.response: I agree that B042 is original and that it has produced a very large literature, and it is my first alternative for that reason. I still place it behind B012 for maturity rather than for merit: the 2018 experiments are only about eight years old, the superconducting mechanism is unsettled, and several of us (Johansson, Mehlig, Eriksson) flagged sample dependence and the divided experimental credit among Jarillo-Herrero, Cao, Dean, Kim and others. A prize that is correct in its first sentence but whose citation has to avoid saying what the superconductivity is carries more risk than one for an instrument that is already working at its quoted accuracy. Pearce's own attribution paragraph, theory pair plus one experimental group, is persuasive, and if the committee judges the field mature enough I would not object to B042 as the lead.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B005) first but flagged that the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits makes another circuit award look repetitive, and ranked the clocks second, stressing that the 2005 comb prize could reduce room for another precision-measurement award.
responses.response: I share the worry about B005 after 2025 and I think Johansson is right to say so as someone close to that community; it is a reason to keep circuit QED out of the preferred configuration this year even though I ranked it third. On the 2005 argument I would answer that the two-way risk is symmetric: the committee did not treat the 2012 prizes as blocking the 2025 circuit award either. What matters is whether the new achievement is a distinct idea, and magic-wavelength trapping is. I do accept Johansson's point that credit for early lattice-clock work by others is not captured, which is why my proposed citation is phrased around the lattice clock concept and its realisation rather than around the first demonstration of any single species.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the clocks first and argued that the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured combs and single-ion control, which lattice clocks build on without duplicating, while flagging that the first demonstrations (strontium versus ytterbium) cannot be verified.
responses.response: I agree with Lindroth on the distinctness argument and on the need for care over who demonstrated what first. Where I would qualify her view is on B030, which she ranked second: the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp candidate is strong in maturity, but Olsson and Mehlig both note that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the 3D topological-insulator experimenters, are missing from the credited names. That is a more serious attribution gap than the ones attached to the clocks, so I would not put B030 into the preferred configuration this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second, and whether an award before it is read as premature.
Whether two names fairly cover the lattice-clock history, given the roles of other groups and of the first demonstrations in different species, which I cannot verify from the files.
Whether B042 is mature enough that the committee would prefer it to B012 this year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B012 (Katori, Ye) from my profile. I am an atomic physicist at Lund and know the optical-physics community generally, but my documented connections (Svanberg, Aldén, Hall's laboratory in Boulder, Rippe, Walther, Kinos, WACQT, Deep Light Vision, European quantum-memory collaborations) do not include the candidates, although my stay in John Hall's laboratory is in the same broad laser-metrology milieu as JILA. I would flag my WACQT involvement as a possible recusal issue for B005 and, more loosely, for B020 and B002, which belong to the quantum-technology community I work in, and I would not push those as the preferred configuration.
